c: Two resistors in a row

Connect two resistors in series across a supply and tap the point where they meet. The voltage at that point is a fixed fraction of the supply. With equal resistors it is exactly half. In general, it is the supply voltage times the bottom resistor divided by the sum of both. A 10 kilohm resistor on top and a 20 kilohm on the bottom across 9 volts gives 6 volts at the middle. Nothing else is involved. The ratio of the two parts sets the output, whatever their absolute values.
Turning resistance into voltage

Many sensors work by changing resistance. A thermistor changes with temperature, a photocell with light, a flex sensor with bending. A microcontroller cannot measure resistance directly. It measures voltage. So you pair the sensor with a fixed resistor to make a divider, and the midpoint voltage now moves as the sensor's resistance moves. The humble divider is the translator between the physical world and the input pin. If you ever wire a light sensor to an Arduino, this is the circuit you are building.
A volume knob is a divider

A potentiometer is a strip of resistive material with a sliding contact. The two ends go across the signal and the slider picks off a fraction of it. Turning the knob changes the ratio of the resistance above the slider to the resistance below it. That is a voltage divider you adjust by hand. Volume controls, light dimmer inputs, joysticks and the position sensors in older throttle pedals all work this way. One part gives you every ratio from zero to one.
Stepping signals down safely

Dividers also shrink voltages to levels a chip can accept. A 5 volt sensor output feeding a 3.3 volt input pin can pass through a 10 kilohm and 20 kilohm divider and arrive at 3.3 volts. A 12 volt battery can be measured by a chip that tolerates only 3.3 volts by dividing by four or more first. The chip reads the smaller number and the software multiplies it back up. This is how nearly every battery gauge senses its own pack voltage.
The catch: loading

A divider only holds its ratio if almost no current is drawn from the midpoint. Whatever you connect there is effectively in parallel with the bottom resistor, which changes the ratio. Feed a motor from a divider and the voltage collapses. The rule of thumb is that the load should have at least ten times the resistance of the divider's resistors. That is why a divider is fine for signals and references, and why you never use one to power anything. Power needs a regulator, which adjusts itself as the load changes.
Dividers you did not mean to build

Dividers also appear by accident. A corroded connector adds a few ohms in series with a load, and the supply voltage is now shared between the corrosion and the load. The load sees less than it should, and the bad connection gets warm. A weak battery behaves the same way: its internal resistance rises with age, so it measures fine with nothing attached and sags the moment a motor asks for current. Mechanics chase this fault constantly. Measuring the voltage at the load while it is running, not at the battery while idle, exposes it.
Choosing the values

Small resistors make a stiff divider that tolerates loading but wastes current all day. Large ones save power but become sensitive to loading and electrical noise. For signals into a microcontroller, values between 1 kilohm and 100 kilohms are the usual range, with 10 kilohms the common default. In battery gadgets designers push toward hundreds of kilohms to save every microamp. When you see two resistors in series with a wire leaving from between them on a schematic, you now know what you are looking at.
It blocks a brake

While you are awake, a substance called adenosine accumulates in the brain and attaches to receptors that make you feel progressively sleepier. Caffeine has a similar shape. It fits into the same receptors without activating them, so the adenosine cannot deliver its message. You feel more alert because a brake has been disabled, not because fuel has been added. The adenosine is still there. When the caffeine clears, it floods back, which is the afternoon crash.
How long it lasts

Caffeine is absorbed quickly and reaches its peak in the blood within about an hour. The body then removes it slowly. The half-life, the time for half of a dose to be cleared, averages about five hours in healthy adults and ranges widely, from roughly two to ten. Genetics, smoking, pregnancy and some medicines all shift it. So a coffee at 4 in the afternoon may leave a quarter of its caffeine still at work at 2 in the morning.
How much is in what

A typical mug of brewed coffee contains somewhere around 80 to 100 milligrams of caffeine, though strength varies widely between cafes and brewing methods. A single shot of espresso has about 60 to 65. A cup of black tea has 40 to 50, and green tea somewhat less. A can of cola has 30 to 40. Energy drinks range from about 80 to more than 300 per can, so the label is worth reading. Decaffeinated coffee is not caffeine free, containing a few milligrams a cup. Dark chocolate contributes a little as well, and so do some pain relief tablets.
The usual ceiling

The United States Food and Drug Administration cites 400 milligrams a day, roughly four cups of brewed coffee, as an amount not generally associated with harmful effects in healthy adults. Sensitivity varies a great deal. Some people feel jittery and anxious on one cup. Advice for pregnancy is lower, and anyone pregnant or with a heart rhythm problem should follow their clinician's guidance. Pure caffeine powder is dangerous, because a lethal amount fits on a spoon.
Tolerance and withdrawal

With daily use, the brain compensates by making more adenosine receptors. The same dose then produces less effect, and regular drinkers need their morning cup simply to feel normal. Stop suddenly and the surplus receptors have nothing blocking them. The result is a headache, fatigue and irritability beginning within about a day and lasting up to a week or so. Cutting down gradually over a couple of weeks avoids most of it. Weekend headaches in people who drink a lot of coffee at work and little at home are often withdrawal.
Performance

Caffeine is one of the few supplements with solid evidence behind it. It improves endurance, reaction time and alertness, and it is permitted in sport. The effect is clearest when you are tired or under-slept. It does not replace sleep, however. It masks sleepiness while judgement and memory remain impaired, which matters if you are driving. A short nap taken right after a coffee, timed so the caffeine arrives as you wake, is a well-tested trick for long drives.
Using it well

A few rules get most of the benefit. Have your last caffeine at least eight hours before bed. Wait an hour or so after waking for the first cup if you find it helps you avoid an afternoon slump. Do not use it to push through chronic tiredness, which is a problem to solve, not to cover. And take an occasional week at a lower dose, which restores the effect of the amount you normally drink.
The illusion of knowing

Rereading a chapter feels effective. The words are familiar, the ideas flow and you finish with a sense of mastery. That feeling is produced by recognition, which is much easier than recall. Recognizing a sentence you have seen before tells you almost nothing about whether you could produce the idea unprompted. Students consistently predict that rereading will serve them best, and experiments consistently show they are wrong. Familiarity is being mistaken for knowledge. Highlighting has the same weakness. It feels like work and leaves you with a colourful page and very little that you could repeat without it.
The key experiment

In a well-known study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke, students read a short passage. Some then read it again. Others closed the text and wrote down everything they could remember. Tested after five minutes, the rereaders did slightly better. Tested a week later, the result reversed. Those who had practised recalling remembered substantially more, around 60 percent of the material against about 40 percent for repeated study in one version of the experiment. The rereaders had been more confident.
Why recall strengthens memory

Retrieving a memory is not like reading a file. The act changes the memory, strengthening the path that leads to it and tying it to more cues. Each successful retrieval makes the next one easier. Reading the answer does not exercise that path at all. It also explains why a failed attempt still helps. Trying to recall something, failing, and then checking the answer produces better learning than being shown the answer at once, because the attempt prepared the ground.
Feedback matters

Testing yourself works best when you find out whether you were right. Without feedback you may rehearse an error and make it stronger. The fix is easy: check your answer against the source after each attempt, and pay particular attention to anything you got wrong with confidence. Those are the most valuable items. Mistakes made confidently and then corrected tend to be remembered especially well, a finding researchers call the hypercorrection effect.
Ways to do it

You do not need formal tests. Close the book and write a summary from memory. Explain the idea aloud to an imaginary listener. Turn headings into questions and answer them before reading the section. Use flashcards, and say the answer before turning the card. At the end of a lecture or meeting, spend two minutes writing the main points without looking at your notes. Each of these replaces passive exposure with an act of recall. None needs special materials, and each takes only a few minutes at the end of a study session or a working day.
Explain it simply

A demanding form of retrieval is trying to teach the idea in plain language, without jargon, as if to a twelve-year-old. Wherever you find yourself falling back on a technical term or waving your hands, you have found the gap in your own understanding. Go back to the source for that part alone, then try again. The method is often associated with the physicist Richard Feynman, who had a reputation for being able to explain difficult things clearly.
The cost and the payoff

Self-testing is less pleasant than rereading. It exposes what you do not know, and it is slower per page. This is why most people avoid it, and why it gives an advantage to those who do not. The practical rule is to spend more of your study time with the book closed than open. Read once, carefully. Then spend the remaining time trying to produce the material from memory, checking, and trying again a few days later. It will feel less comfortable and you will learn more.
What it is for

An emergency fund is money held in cash for one purpose: to cover you when something goes wrong. A job ends. A car fails. A roof leaks. A medical bill arrives. These events are not rare. Across a decade, nearly everyone meets several. The fund is not an investment and should not be judged as one. Its return is measured in the expensive things you avoid doing: running up a credit card, borrowing at a high rate, or selling long-term investments at whatever price the market happens to offer that week.
How much

The usual guidance is three to six months of essential expenses. The word essential matters. Count rent or mortgage, food, utilities, insurance, transport and minimum debt payments, not your full current spending. Where you fall in the range depends on how exposed you are. A household with two steady incomes can sit near three months. A single earner, a freelancer with uneven income or someone in a volatile industry should lean toward six or more. If the full target feels unreachable, a first goal of one month still changes a great deal.
Where to keep it

The fund needs to be safe and quickly reachable, in that order of priority over yield. A savings account at an insured bank is the standard home. Keeping it in a separate account from everyday spending helps, because money you can see in your checking balance tends to get spent. It should not sit in shares, where it might be down by a third at the very moment a recession costs you your job. Those two things tend to happen together, which is the entire problem.
The cost of not having one

Without a cushion, a small shock becomes an expensive one. A 1,500 dollar repair put on a card at 22 percent and paid off slowly can cost several hundred dollars in interest. Missing a payment adds fees and damages your credit record, which raises the cost of future borrowing. People without savings also make worse decisions under pressure: accepting the first job offered, or keeping a failing car because they cannot fund the alternative. Cash buys time, and time usually buys a better choice.
Fund or debt first

A common puzzle is whether to build savings or pay down debt. A sensible order many advisers suggest is this. First build a small starter fund, perhaps a month of expenses, so that the next surprise does not go straight onto a card. Then attack high-interest debt aggressively, because nothing safe pays as much as that debt costs. Then return to finish the full fund. Throughout, take any employer matching contribution to a retirement plan, since that is an immediate return you cannot get elsewhere.
What counts as an emergency

The fund fails if it becomes a general spending account. An emergency is unexpected, necessary and urgent. A holiday is not, however much you need one. Neither is a sale. Annual bills that you know are coming, such as insurance premiums or car registration, are not emergencies either. They are predictable and deserve their own small savings pot. Keeping the definition strict is what ensures the money is still there on the day a real emergency arrives.
The part nobody mentions

The largest benefit is psychological. Knowing that you could cover several months without income changes how you behave. You can negotiate at work without fear, leave a bad situation, or take a sensible risk. Financial stress narrows attention and worsens judgement, and a cushion relieves it. People who have built one often describe the feeling as lighter, not richer. For money that sits in an account doing almost nothing, that is a considerable return.
Looking past the current bet

Pot odds measure the money in the middle now. Implied odds add the money you expect to win on later streets if you make your hand. Suppose you face a bet of 20 into 40 with a draw that hits about 18 percent of the time. You need 25 percent, so the call looks wrong. But if your opponent will pay you another 100 when you hit, you are really risking 20 to win 160. That needs only about 11 percent, and the call becomes clearly profitable.
Set mining is the classic case

Small and medium pocket pairs are the textbook example. You will flop three of a kind or better about 12 percent of the time, roughly one flop in eight and a half. The immediate pot odds before the flop almost never justify a call on that basis. The call makes sense because a flopped set is well hidden and often wins a very large pot. A common guideline is that you and your opponent should each have at least 15 to 20 times the size of the call behind for the play to pay.
Stack depth decides everything

Implied odds are limited by the smaller stack in the hand. If your opponent has only 60 dollars left and you must call 20, the most you can win later is 60, however perfectly you hit. This is why speculative hands such as small pairs and suited connectors gain value when stacks are deep and lose it when stacks are short. In a tournament with ten big blinds, those hands are nearly worthless. With 200 big blinds in a cash game, they are among the most profitable.
Hidden hands get paid, obvious ones do not

The value of hitting depends on whether your opponent can see it coming. A set is disguised, since nobody can tell from the board that you hold a pair in your hand. A straight made with connected cards is often disguised too. A flush is the opposite. When the third card of a suit lands, everyone notices, and a careful opponent slows down. So flush draws have weaker implied odds than players assume, and a draw to anything but the highest flush can cost you money when a bigger one is out.
The opponent matters most

Implied odds are a prediction about another person. Against a player who cannot fold top pair, they are enormous. Against a cautious player who gives up the moment the board turns frightening, they barely exist. Before making a call that depends on future winnings, ask what this particular opponent does with a good but second best hand. If the answer is that they keep betting or keep calling, call. If they shut down, you are paying full price for a prize you will not collect.
Reverse implied odds

The idea also runs backwards. Some hands tend to win small pots and lose big ones. Hold king jack on a king high flop and you will often win a little when you are ahead and lose a lot when someone holds ace king or king queen. A weak flush draw has the same problem when it gets there against a bigger flush. These are reverse implied odds: the money you expect to lose later when your hand improves to second best. Dominated hands are the main culprits.
An honest test

Implied odds are the most abused concept in poker, because they can excuse any call. To keep yourself honest, state the amount out loud: how much more must I win, on average, when I hit, for this call to break even? Then ask whether this opponent, with these stacks, on this kind of board, will really pay that. If you cannot say yes with a straight face, the call is not about implied odds. It is about wanting to see another card.
A long search for the gene

By the early twentieth century, biologists knew that traits were inherited in discrete units called genes and that genes sat on chromosomes in the cell nucleus. What genes were made of was unknown. Chromosomes contain both protein and a substance called DNA, first isolated in 1869. Most scientists bet on protein, which seemed complex enough for the job. Experiments in the 1940s and early 1950s, using bacteria and the viruses that infect them, showed that the genetic material was in fact DNA.
The double helix

The structure was worked out in 1953 by James Watson and Francis Crick in Cambridge. They relied heavily on X-ray images of DNA made in London by Rosalind Franklin and her student, shown to them without her knowledge, and on measurements from Maurice Wilkins. Watson, Crick and Wilkins received a Nobel Prize in 1962. Franklin had died of cancer four years earlier, and the prize is not awarded after death. Her contribution has been far more fully acknowledged since.
A ladder with four kinds of rung

DNA is shaped like a twisted ladder. The two side rails are chains of sugar and phosphate. The rungs are pairs of chemical units called bases, of which there are four: adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine, written A, T, G and C. They pair by a strict rule. A always joins with T, and G always joins with C. So the sequence along one rail fixes the sequence along the other. If one side reads A, G, T, the other must read T, C, A.
Copying follows from the shape

That pairing rule explains how genetic information is copied. When a cell divides, the ladder unzips down the middle. Each half then serves as a template, and new bases attach according to the rule, producing two identical ladders where there was one. Watson and Crick noted this in a famously understated sentence at the end of their paper. The copying is extremely accurate but not perfect, and the rare errors, called mutations, are the raw material of evolution.
From letters to proteins

The sequence of bases is a code. Read three letters at a time, each triplet specifies one of twenty amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. A gene is a stretch of DNA that spells out one protein, and proteins do most of the work in a cell, from digesting food to carrying oxygen. With four letters taken three at a time there are 64 possible triplets for 20 amino acids, so most amino acids have more than one spelling. Nearly all living things use the same code.
The scale of it

The human genome is about three billion base pairs long. Stretched out, the DNA in a single human cell would measure roughly two metres, packed into a nucleus a few thousandths of a millimetre across. It contains around twenty thousand genes that code for proteins, far fewer than scientists expected, and a great deal of DNA that regulates when and where those genes are used. Any two people differ in only about one letter in a thousand.
Reading and writing

The first full reading of a human genome, completed in the early 2000s, took over a decade and cost on the order of three billion dollars. Machines can now do it in about a day for well under a thousand dollars. That collapse in cost underlies ancestry tests, the identification of inherited diseases, forensic evidence and the tracking of viruses as they mutate. Tools for editing DNA have followed. Knowing the structure was the start of being able to read the instructions, and reading them was the start of changing them.
Two kinds of flow

Direct current, DC, flows in one direction, like water down a river. Batteries, solar panels and USB ports supply DC. Alternating current, AC, flows back and forth, reversing direction on a regular beat. The power from a wall socket is AC. In North America it completes 60 full cycles a second and in most of the rest of the world it completes 50. Nearly all electronics run on DC inside, which is why almost everything you plug in begins by converting one into the other.
Why the grid chose AC

In the 1880s, Thomas Edison's DC systems and the AC systems backed by George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla competed to electrify cities. AC won for one practical reason: the transformer. A transformer changes AC voltage up or down with nothing but two coils of wire around an iron core. That let power stations send electricity at high voltage, where little is lost in the wires, and step it down near homes. DC had no equally simple way to change voltage at the time, so DC stations had to sit within a mile or so of their customers.
What the wall numbers mean

A North American socket is called 120 volts, but the voltage is a smooth wave that swings to about plus 170 volts and back to minus 170. The 120 figure is the RMS value, the steady DC voltage that would deliver the same heating power. Most of Europe, Asia and Africa use about 230 volts RMS. Higher voltage means less current for the same power, which is why a kettle in Britain boils noticeably faster than one in the United States on an ordinary socket.
Turning AC into DC

A power adapter does the conversion in stages. A transformer or switching stage brings the voltage down. Diodes, which pass current in one direction only, flip the negative half of the wave so that it all points the same way. That step is called rectifying. A large capacitor then fills in the gaps between the bumps, and a regulator trims the result to a steady figure such as 5 volts. Old adapters were heavy because they used iron transformers. Modern ones are small because they switch at high frequency, which needs far less iron.
DC is making a comeback

The grid is AC, but more and more of what connects to it is DC by nature. Solar panels make DC. Batteries store DC. LEDs, computers and electric car motors' controllers run on DC. Modern power electronics can now change DC voltages efficiently, the thing Edison lacked. That is why very long transmission links increasingly use high voltage DC, and why USB has quietly become a household DC standard, delivering up to 240 watts in its latest version, enough for a laptop or a monitor.
Frequency and why plugs differ

The number of cycles a second is called frequency and is measured in hertz. Clocks and motors once relied on it for timing, which is one reason an appliance built for one country may misbehave in another even with a plug adapter. Voltage is the bigger hazard. A 120 volt hair dryer on a 230 volt socket draws about four times its rated power for a moment and then fails, sometimes dramatically. Most phone and laptop chargers are marked 100 to 240 volts and work anywhere. Read the small print on the label before you travel.
What matters at the bench

Three practical points follow. First, polarity matters on DC: connect a part backwards and it may be destroyed, so check the plus and minus marks. Second, mains AC is dangerous in a way small DC supplies are not. Work on the low voltage side of an adapter and leave the wall side closed unless you are trained. Third, when a multimeter reads nonsense, check its dial. Measuring a battery on the AC setting or a socket on the DC setting produces numbers that look almost plausible and mean nothing.
Where the rule came from

The advice to drink eight glasses of water a day is repeated everywhere and has no clear scientific origin. One likely source is a 1945 American recommendation that adults need about 2.5 litres of water daily. The next sentence, usually forgotten, said that most of this is contained in prepared foods. Reviews by physicians looking for evidence behind the eight-glass rule have come up empty. It is not harmful advice for most people. It is simply not a requirement. Carrying a large bottle everywhere became fashionable long after the rule appeared, not because new evidence arrived.
What the body needs

Needs vary with body size, activity, climate and diet. The United States National Academies have suggested an adequate total intake of about 3.7 litres a day for men and 2.7 for women. The important word is total. That figure includes water from all drinks and from food, which typically supplies around a fifth of it. Fruit, vegetables, soup and even bread contain a good deal of water. Nobody needs to drink the whole amount from a bottle.
Thirst works

Your body regulates its water content tightly. When the concentration of your blood rises by even one or two percent, the brain triggers thirst and tells the kidneys to hold water back. For healthy people in ordinary conditions, drinking when thirsty and with meals is enough. The claim that by the time you feel thirsty you are already dangerously dehydrated is not supported. Thirst arrives well before any harm, which is precisely what it evolved to do.
Coffee and tea count

Caffeine is a mild diuretic, which led to the belief that coffee and tea dehydrate you. In people who drink them regularly, the effect is small, and the water in the cup far outweighs it. Studies comparing moderate coffee intake with the same volume of water have found no meaningful difference in hydration. Milk, juice and sparkling water all count as well. Alcohol is the real exception, since it suppresses the hormone that tells the kidneys to conserve water.
A simple check

The colour of your urine is a practical gauge. Pale yellow, like straw, indicates you are well hydrated. Dark yellow or amber suggests you need more fluid. Completely clear usually means you are drinking more than you need. Some vitamins and foods change the colour, so it is a rough guide. Other signs of needing water are a dry mouth, headache, tiredness and passing urine only a few times in a day. A mild headache late in a busy afternoon is quite often nothing more than a morning without a drink.
When to drink more

Thirst is less reliable in some situations. Older adults often have a weaker thirst response and can become dehydrated without noticing. Hard exercise, hot weather, fever, vomiting and diarrhoea all raise losses quickly. In those cases, drink on a schedule. During long, sweaty exertion, some salt matters too, because sweat carries sodium out with the water. Persistent vomiting or diarrhoea, especially in a small child or an elderly person, needs medical attention.
Too much is possible

Drinking far more than you lose can dilute the sodium in your blood to dangerous levels, a condition called hyponatraemia. It has killed marathon runners and military recruits who were told to drink as much as possible. The modern advice for endurance events is to drink to thirst, not to a fixed plan. For everyday life, there is no benefit in forcing down water you do not want. Keep a glass within reach, drink when you feel like it and let the kidneys do the arithmetic.
A mood problem in disguise

People who procrastinate usually know exactly what they should be doing and how long they have. Better calendars rarely help. Psychologists who study the behaviour, among them Timothy Pychyl and Fuschia Sirois, describe it as a problem of emotion regulation. The task brings up something unpleasant, such as boredom, anxiety, self-doubt or resentment. Avoiding the task makes the feeling go away at once. The relief is the reward, and it teaches you to avoid again next time. Seen this way, procrastination is a habit like any other, with a cue, a routine and a payoff.
The present self wins

The trade is lopsided because the relief is immediate and the cost is delayed. Humans weigh the present far more heavily than the future, a tendency economists call present bias. The person who will face the deadline next week feels like someone else, a stranger who can be handed the problem. Brain imaging studies have found that people thinking about their future selves show patterns closer to those seen when thinking about another person than about themselves.
What makes a task avoidable

Certain features make a task more likely to be put off. It is vague, so you do not know where to start. It is large, with no visible end. It is boring, or it is difficult. It matters a great deal, which raises the stakes of doing it badly. Or it was imposed by someone else. Notice that importance makes procrastination worse, not better. This is why people clean the kitchen thoroughly on the day they are supposed to begin a report that could affect their career.
Shrink the first step

The most dependable tactic is to reduce the task until starting takes no courage. Do not write the report. Open the document and write a bad first sentence. Do not do your taxes. Find last year's return and put it on the table. The unpleasant feeling is concentrated at the threshold. Once you are a few minutes in, the task is almost always less awful than you expected, and continuing is far easier than beginning was.
Promise only five minutes

A related device is the five-minute bargain. Tell yourself you will work on the thing for five minutes and are then free to stop. Mean it. Most of the time you will carry on, because the hard part was starting. On the days you do stop, you have still done five minutes and kept the promise, which protects your trust in your own agreements. That trust is worth more than any single session.
Be less hard on yourself

It seems obvious that harsh self-criticism should cure procrastination. Studies suggest the opposite. In research on students, those who forgave themselves for putting off studying before one exam procrastinated less before the next. Self-blame adds another bad feeling to the task, and bad feelings are what you were avoiding in the first place. Treating a lapse as information, not as a verdict on your character, makes it easier to return to the work.
Change the surroundings

Finally, make avoiding harder and starting easier. Decide the night before what the first task will be and leave it open on your desk. Work somewhere the usual escapes are out of reach. Tell someone what you will finish by when, since an expectation from another person is a strong motivator. None of this removes the uncomfortable feeling. It only lowers the barrier enough that you start anyway, and starting is nearly always the cure. Expect to need the trick again tomorrow. That is normal.
The default is the trap

Credit card statements show a minimum payment, usually a small percentage of the balance. Paying only that keeps the account in good standing and keeps you in debt for a very long time. Because the minimum shrinks as the balance shrinks, most of each payment goes to interest, and the balance barely moves. A balance of a few thousand dollars repaid at the minimum can take well over a decade to clear and cost more in interest than the original purchases. The minimum is designed for the lender's benefit.
List everything first

Any plan starts with a list. Write down every debt: who is owed, the balance, the interest rate and the minimum payment. People often avoid this step because the total is unpleasant to look at. It is still the step that makes the rest possible. The list usually contains surprises, such as a store card charging more than 25 percent or a small loan that could be cleared in two months. Add up the minimums. Whatever you can pay above that total is your weapon.
The avalanche

In the avalanche method, you pay the minimum on every debt and put all extra money toward the one with the highest interest rate. When that is gone, you move to the next highest. Mathematically this is the cheapest and fastest route, because each extra dollar is cancelling the most expensive interest available. The drawback is that the highest-rate debt may also be a large one, and you can work for many months without the satisfaction of closing an account.
The snowball

In the snowball method, you ignore interest rates and attack the smallest balance first. When it is cleared, you roll its payment into the next smallest. It costs somewhat more in interest than the avalanche. Its advantage is momentum. Accounts close quickly, the list gets shorter, and each success frees a larger payment for the next. Research on people repaying real debts has found that closing accounts keeps them motivated, which matters because the cheapest plan is worthless if you abandon it.
Choosing between them

If your debts have widely different rates, say a card at 24 percent and a car loan at 6, the avalanche saves real money and is worth the patience. If the rates are similar, the two methods cost nearly the same and you may as well take the motivational boost of the snowball. A reasonable blend is to clear one or two tiny balances for the quick win and then switch to highest rate first. The best method is the one you will still be following in eighteen months.
Lowering the rate

While paying down, look for ways to cut the interest itself. A balance transfer card with a low introductory rate can help if you can clear the balance before the offer ends and you account for the transfer fee. A personal loan at a lower fixed rate can replace several cards with one payment. Calling a lender and asking for a lower rate sometimes works. None of these fix anything unless the spending that built the debt changes too. Otherwise the cleared cards simply fill again.
Not all debt is equal

A mortgage at a low fixed rate and a credit card at 22 percent are different creatures. The urgent target is high-interest consumer debt, where no ordinary investment can match what the debt costs you. Low-rate, long-term debt can reasonably sit alongside saving and investing. A rough test is to compare the rate on the debt with what you could realistically earn elsewhere. If the debt costs clearly more, paying it off is the best guaranteed return available to you.
Two ways to win

When you check or call, you can only win by showing down the best hand. When you bet or raise, you add a second path: your opponent may fold. Fold equity is the value of that second path, the share of the pot you pick up simply because the other player gives in. It is the reason aggressive poker beats passive poker over time. The passive player needs the best cards. The aggressive player needs either the best cards or an opponent who is not willing to continue.
How often a bluff must work

The arithmetic for a pure bluff is short. Divide your bet by the total of the pot plus your bet. A bet of half the pot must succeed one time in three. A bet of two thirds of the pot must work 40 percent of the time. A pot-sized bet needs to work half the time. A bet of one third of the pot needs only one fold in four. Smaller bluffs need to work less often but are easier to call, so the two effects pull against each other.
The semi-bluff adds a third way

A semi-bluff is a bet with a hand that is probably behind now but can improve, such as a flush draw. It wins if the opponent folds, and it can still win if they call and you hit. Take a pot of 100 and a bet of 100. If the opponent folds 40 percent of the time and you have 35 percent equity when called, the play earns about 43 dollars on average. With no equity at all, the same bet would lose 20. The draw turns a losing bluff into a strong play.
Who you bet into matters

Fold equity is a property of the opponent, not of your cards. Some players call far too much and almost never fold a pair. Against them your fold equity is close to zero, and bluffing is setting money on fire. Others fold too readily when the bet is large or the board is frightening. Against them, hands with no showdown value at all become profitable bets. The first adjustment a thinking player makes at any table is deciding which kind of opponent is in each seat.
Your image and your story

People fold when the bet is believable. A player who has been caught bluffing twice in the last hour has little fold equity for a while. One who has shown down only strong hands has plenty. The line you take in the hand matters too. A bluff is credible when your earlier actions fit the strong hand you are now representing. A sudden large bet on the river from someone who checked every street before it tells a story that does not add up, and observant opponents call it.
Short stacks lose it

Fold equity shrinks as your stack does. A raise only frightens someone if it puts meaningful chips at risk. In a tournament, a player with fifteen big blinds who moves all in can still force folds from hands that do not want to gamble. A player with four big blinds cannot, because calling costs so little that almost any hand is priced in. This is why waiting too long to make a move with a dwindling stack is a mistake: you give up the weapon before you use it.
The takeaway

Every time you consider betting, estimate two numbers. How often does this opponent fold to this bet? How much equity do I have when they do not? If the folds alone make the bet profitable, your cards hardly matter. If they do not, you need real equity to make up the difference. Players who only bet when they have a hand are easy to read and easy to beat. Players who understand fold equity win pots that their cards alone never would.
The problem of too many elements

By the 1860s, chemists had identified about sixty elements, substances that cannot be broken down into anything simpler. Each had its own weight, appearance and behaviour, and there seemed to be no order to them. Some patterns were known. Lithium, sodium and potassium all reacted violently with water. Chlorine, bromine and iodine formed similar salts. But nobody had a scheme that fitted every element, and textbooks simply listed them. Students had to memorize each one separately, with no way to guess how an unfamiliar element would behave.
Mendeleev's cards

In 1869, Dmitri Mendeleev, a professor in St Petersburg writing a textbook, wrote each element on a card with its atomic weight and properties and laid the cards out in order of weight. He saw that the properties repeated at regular intervals. Arranged in rows so that similar elements fell in the same column, the elements formed a table. Others had noticed parts of the pattern. Mendeleev went further than any of them, and the reason is what he did next.
The gaps

Where the pattern required an element that did not exist, Mendeleev left a blank and insisted that an undiscovered element belonged there. He went on to predict the properties of three of them in detail, including their weights and densities. Gallium was discovered in 1875, scandium in 1879 and germanium in 1886, and each matched his forecasts closely. A scheme that merely organizes known facts is a convenience. One that predicts unknown ones correctly is a discovery about nature.
The real ordering principle

Mendeleev ordered by weight, and in a few places he had to swap elements against the weight order to keep the columns sensible. The reason became clear in 1913, when the young English physicist Henry Moseley showed that each element has a whole number, the atomic number, equal to the count of protons in its nucleus. Ordered by that number, the table has no exceptions. Moseley was killed in the First World War two years later, at the age of 27.
Why the pattern repeats

The explanation for the repetition came from the physics of the atom. Electrons surround the nucleus in layers called shells, and an atom's chemistry is governed mainly by the electrons in its outermost shell. Elements in the same column have the same number of outer electrons, so they behave alike. Sodium and potassium each have one, which they give up readily. The noble gases on the far right have full outer shells, which is why helium and neon react with almost nothing.
Reading the table

The rows are called periods and the columns groups. Metals occupy the left and centre, non-metals the upper right. Moving across a row, atoms hold their electrons more tightly. Moving down a column, atoms get larger and, among the metals, generally more reactive. From an element's position alone, a chemist can make a fair guess at whether it conducts electricity, what it combines with and in what proportions. That is an extraordinary amount of information for one chart.
Still growing

The table now holds 118 elements. About ninety occur naturally on Earth. The rest have been made in laboratories and reactors, the heaviest of them a few atoms at a time, lasting only fractions of a second before decaying. The four most recent additions received their official names in 2016. Whether still heavier elements can exist long enough to be detected is an open research question. The chart on every classroom wall is unfinished at one end.
What a resistor is for

A resistor does one thing: it resists current by a known amount. That single ability covers a surprising range of jobs. It limits the current into an LED so the LED survives. It sets the gain of an amplifier. It holds an unused input pin at a definite level. It turns a current into a voltage so that a chip can measure it. A typical circuit board carries more resistors than any other part. They cost a fraction of a cent each in quantity, which is why designers reach for one whenever a current needs taming.
Reading the colour bands

Through-hole resistors carry coloured bands because numbers would be too small to print. The colours stand for digits: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, grey 8, white 9. On a four band part, the first two bands are digits and the third is the number of zeros to add. Yellow, violet, red reads 4, 7 and two zeros: 4,700 ohms, or 4.7 kilohms. The last band, set slightly apart, gives the tolerance. Gold means 5 percent, brown 1 percent.
Surface mount codes

The tiny rectangular resistors on modern boards use printed numbers. A three digit code works like the bands: two digits and a count of zeros. So 103 means 10 followed by three zeros, 10,000 ohms. 472 is 4,700 ohms. The letter R marks a decimal point, so 4R7 is 4.7 ohms. A part marked 0 or 000 is a zero ohm link, a resistor shaped wire that lets a machine place a jumper. The smallest sizes carry no marking at all, and the only way to identify one is to measure it.
Why the values look odd

Resistors come in values such as 10, 22, 33, 47 and 68, repeated at every power of ten. The numbers look arbitrary but are spaced so that each is roughly the same percentage above the last. With 5 percent parts, the ranges of neighbouring values just touch, so every possible resistance is covered by something on the shelf. The standard set is called the E series. You rarely need an exact value. Pick the nearest standard one, and if precision matters, pick a tighter tolerance.
Tolerance and what it costs

A 5 percent, 1 kilohm resistor may really be anywhere from 950 to 1,050 ohms. For limiting LED current or pulling a pin high, that is irrelevant. For a voltage divider that sets a measurement, it matters, because the error passes straight into the reading. One percent parts cost almost nothing extra today and are the sensible default. Precision references and instrument inputs use 0.1 percent parts that also drift very little as they warm up. Buy accuracy only where the circuit's result depends on it.
The power rating is the other number

Size tells you how much heat a resistor can shed. The common through-hole part handles a quarter of a watt. The tiny surface mount ones handle a tenth or less. Work out the power with voltage squared divided by resistance and stay under half the rating. A resistor asked to dissipate too much does not fail politely. It discolours, drifts upward in value, and eventually cracks or chars the board beneath it. If you find a scorched patch on an old circuit board, there was usually a hard working resistor above it.
Three mistakes to skip

First, measuring a resistor while it is still in a powered circuit, which gives nonsense and can damage the meter. Power off first. Second, measuring it in circuit and trusting the number: other parts in parallel pull the reading down, so lift one leg if it matters. Third, holding both leads with your fingers on a high value part. Your skin is a resistor of a few hundred kilohms to a few megohms, and it is now in parallel with the thing you are trying to measure.
The deck is finite

There are 1,326 different two-card starting hands in hold'em. They are not equally represented. Any specific pocket pair, such as two kings, can be dealt 6 ways. Any specific unpaired hand, such as ace king, can be dealt 16 ways: 4 of them suited and 12 offsuit. So before any cards are seen, an opponent is dealt ace king nearly three times as often as a pair of aces. Hand reading begins with these three numbers: 6, 4 and 12.
How often premium hands arrive

The same counting tells you how rare good hands are. You will be dealt a pair of aces once in 221 hands. Any pocket pair comes about once in 17 hands. Ace king, suited or not, arrives roughly once in 83. Two suited cards show up a little under a quarter of the time. A player who complains of never getting aces is usually describing an ordinary night, since at a live table of about 30 hands an hour, aces are due about once every seven hours.
Cards you see remove combinations

Every visible card shrinks the count. If you hold an ace, only three aces remain, and the ways an opponent can hold two of them drop from 6 to 3. The ways they can hold ace king fall from 16 to 12. If an ace is also on the board, pocket aces drop to a single combination. This effect is called card removal, and the cards in your own hand that reduce an opponent's strong holdings are called blockers.
Sets against top pair

Counting changes how a board looks. On a flop of king, seven, two, a player might hold a set. There are three ways each to hold kings, sevens or twos, nine in all. The same player could hold ace king, top pair with the best kicker, in 12 ways. So even before considering how they played the hand, top pair hands outnumber sets. When an opponent raises and you fear the monster, counting reminds you that the monster is usually the less likely holding.
Draws are numerous

On a board with two hearts, think about how many flush draws exist. An opponent could hold any two of the eleven remaining hearts, which is 55 combinations, though most players only play a fraction of those. Straight draws add more. This is why boards with connected or suited cards are called wet: they multiply the number of hands that want to continue. On a dry board such as king, seven, two of three suits, almost no draws exist, and a bet represents a made hand or a pure bluff.
Value hands against bluffs

Combination counting matters most on the river. Suppose an opponent's line is consistent with 10 combinations of strong hands and 5 combinations of missed draws they would bluff with. A third of the time you face a bluff. If the bet is half the pot, you need to be right only 25 percent of the time, so calling is correct. Shift the count to 15 value hands and 2 bluffs and the same call loses badly. The decision comes from the ratio.
Practise on hands you already played

You will not count precisely during play. Train afterwards. Take one hand a session, write down the hands your opponent could plausibly hold, and count the combinations of each. Within a few weeks you start to see boards differently. A scary card stops being scary when you realise it completes only four combinations. A harmless-looking card becomes dangerous when it completes thirty. That shift, from picturing one hand to weighing many, is what experienced players mean by thinking in ranges.
Two plates and a gap

A capacitor is two conductors separated by an insulator. Push charge onto one plate and an equal charge is repelled from the other, and energy is stored in the electric field between them. The amount it can hold per volt is its capacitance, measured in farads. A farad is enormous, so real parts are rated in microfarads, nanofarads and picofarads, each a thousand times smaller than the last. Unlike a battery, a capacitor stores very little, but it can take in or give out that energy almost instantly.
It resists changes in voltage

The useful way to think of a capacitor is that it hates a sudden change in the voltage across it. To change that voltage, charge must flow in or out, and that takes time. So a capacitor across a power supply fills the dips and absorbs the spikes, like a small reservoir on a water main. This is the most common use of all. Every digital chip has one or more small capacitors right next to its power pins for this reason, and removing them makes otherwise good circuits behave unpredictably.
It passes AC and blocks DC

Apply a steady voltage and a capacitor charges up, then no more current flows. Apply a changing voltage and current keeps flowing in and out as the plates charge and discharge. So a capacitor in series with a signal lets the wiggle through while stopping any steady level underneath it. Audio equipment uses this to pass music between stages that sit at different DC voltages. The higher the frequency, the more easily it passes, which is also why capacitors are the basic ingredient of filters.
Timing with a resistor

A capacitor charged through a resistor takes a predictable time to fill. Multiply the resistance in ohms by the capacitance in farads and you get the time constant in seconds, the time to reach about 63 percent of the supply. Ten kilohms and 100 microfarads gives one second. After five time constants the capacitor is essentially full. This simple pair sets delays, blink rates and the cut-off points of filters. The intermittent setting on windscreen wipers was first built from exactly this arrangement.
The main types

Ceramic capacitors are small, cheap and not polarized, and they cover the range from picofarads to a few tens of microfarads. Electrolytic capacitors pack far more capacitance into a can, hundreds or thousands of microfarads, but they are polarized: one lead must stay more positive than the other. Film capacitors are stable and favoured in audio and mains circuits. Supercapacitors reach whole farads and can run a small circuit for minutes or hours. The type matters as much as the value, so read both before substituting one for another.
Polarity and voltage ratings

An electrolytic capacitor connected backwards, or run above its voltage rating, can fail violently. The can is scored on top so that it splits open instead of bursting. The stripe on the side marks the negative lead. Always pick a voltage rating comfortably above what the circuit applies, usually by half again or more. Old electrolytics dry out with heat and age, and bulging tops on the capacitors near a power supply are one of the most common causes of dead monitors, routers and motherboards.
Respect a charged capacitor

A capacitor holds its charge after the power is removed. Small ones are harmless. Large ones in power supplies, camera flashes, microwave ovens and tube amplifiers can hold a dangerous charge for minutes or longer. Technicians discharge them through a resistor before touching anything and then measure to confirm. Shorting one with a screwdriver works but makes a loud bang and pits the tool. If a device plugs into the wall and you are not sure what is inside, assume the big capacitors are charged until a meter says otherwise.
Skill and luck on different clocks

In one hand, luck decides nearly everything. Over a session, luck still dominates. Over tens of thousands of hands, skill takes over. This mismatch is the central fact of poker life. Your edge is small and the swings around it are large. A good cash game player might win a few big blinds per hundred hands on average, while the typical up and down movement over the same hundred hands is many times larger. The signal is real, but it is buried.
What a downswing looks like

Because of that ratio, long losing stretches are normal even for strong players. Simulations of winning players routinely show losing runs of twenty buy-ins or more somewhere in a large sample of hands. A live player seeing about 30 hands an hour needs years to play a hundred thousand hands. So a live player can run badly for months without doing anything wrong, and can also run well for months while playing poorly. Neither stretch proves much. Online players, who can see several hundred hands an hour across multiple tables, reach meaningful samples far sooner, which is one reason the online game produced so many strong players so quickly.
The bankroll is a tool

A bankroll is money set aside only for poker, separate from rent and savings. Its job is to absorb variance so that a bad run does not end your ability to play. Think of it as a carpenter thinks of tools: working capital, not spending money. If losing your poker money would affect your life, you will play scared, avoid correct but risky plays and make worse decisions. A properly sized bankroll buys the freedom to play well.
Common guidelines

For no-limit cash games, a widely used rule is to keep at least 20 to 30 full buy-ins for the stakes you play. In a game with a 200 dollar buy-in, that is 4,000 to 6,000 dollars. Tournaments swing far more, because most of the prize money goes to the top few places, so serious tournament players keep 100 buy-ins or more. These are conventions, not laws. A recreational player with a job who can reload from income needs less than someone paying bills from winnings.
Move down without shame

The other half of bankroll management is dropping to a smaller game when the roll shrinks. If you fall to 15 buy-ins for your usual stake, move down until you rebuild. Pride makes this hard, and refusing to do it is how talented players go broke. Moving down is not an admission that you cannot beat the bigger game. It is an acknowledgment that variance does not care how good you are and that a player with no chips has no edge at all.
Keep records

Memory is a terrible accountant. People remember big wins and forget steady losses. Write down every session: date, stakes, hours, result. After a few months you will know your real hourly rate and whether particular games, times of day or session lengths cost you money. Many players discover they win in the first three hours and give it back in the fifth and sixth. Without records you are guessing about your own results, and most guesses flatter the guesser.
Judging yourself honestly

With so much noise, how do you know if you are any good? Not from one month's result. Look at large samples, and look at decisions. Review hands, especially the ones you won, and ask whether you would play them the same way again. Ask stronger players. A healthy attitude holds two ideas together: results in the short run are mostly luck, and results in the long run are entirely your responsibility.
A coil with a memory

Any current creates a magnetic field around its wire. Wind the wire into a coil and the fields of the turns add together. Building that field takes energy, and collapsing it gives the energy back. The result is a part that resists changes in current the way a heavy flywheel resists changes in speed. Its strength is called inductance, measured in henries, with real parts usually in microhenries or millihenries. Adding an iron or ferrite core concentrates the field and multiplies the inductance many times over.
The mirror image of a capacitor

A capacitor resists changes in voltage and passes fast signals easily. An inductor resists changes in current and passes steady current easily while opposing fast changes. Put simply, capacitors block DC and inductors block high frequencies. Used together they make filters that select or reject a band of frequencies. An old radio tuning dial moved the plates of a capacitor against a fixed coil to choose a station. The same pairing is still inside every radio, phone and wireless charger made today.
Kickback

Because an inductor insists that its current keep flowing, interrupting that current abruptly has a dramatic effect. The collapsing field generates whatever voltage it needs to keep the current going, often hundreds of volts from a 12 volt circuit. This is how a car's ignition coil makes a spark. It is also how a relay or motor destroys the transistor that switches it. The cure is a diode placed backwards across the coil, called a flyback diode, which gives the current a harmless loop to die away in.
How switching supplies use it

The inductor's stubbornness is what makes efficient power conversion possible. A switching regulator connects an inductor to the supply for a moment, storing energy in its field, then disconnects it and lets the inductor deliver that energy to the output. Doing this hundreds of thousands of times a second, and varying how long the switch stays on, produces a lower or higher voltage with very little wasted as heat. Phone chargers, laptop adapters and the converters on every motherboard work this way.
Transformers are two inductors sharing a field

Wind two coils on the same core and a changing current in the first induces a voltage in the second. The ratio of the turns sets the ratio of the voltages. Ten times the turns on the output gives ten times the voltage and a tenth of the current. Because only a changing field induces anything, transformers work on AC and not on steady DC. They also isolate: no wire connects the input to the output, which is what makes a mains adapter safe to touch on its low voltage side.
Ferrite beads and chokes

An inductor used simply to block unwanted high frequency noise is called a choke. The lump moulded onto many laptop and monitor cables is a ferrite sleeve doing this job, soaking up radio frequency interference travelling along the wire. On circuit boards, tiny ferrite beads sit in series with power lines to keep the noise of one section out of another. They cost almost nothing and are often the difference between a product that passes its radio emissions test and one that fails it.
Reading an inductor's limits

Two ratings matter beyond the inductance. The saturation current is the point at which the core cannot hold any more magnetic field. Past it the inductance collapses and the current shoots up, a common cause of failed power converters. The resistance of the winding is the other, since it wastes power as heat. A physically larger inductor of the same value generally has a higher saturation current and lower resistance. When a design calls for a specific inductor, substitute by all three numbers, never by inductance alone.
Who acts when

Hold'em is played in a circle, and a small disc called the button marks the nominal dealer. After the flop, the player on the button acts last on every round of betting. The two players to the button's left post the forced bets, the small blind and the big blind, and must act first after the flop. Everyone else sits somewhere between. Seats that act early are called early position, and the seats just before the button are late position, the cutoff and the hijack.
Information is the advantage

Acting last means you see what everyone else does before you decide. If they check, they have told you something. If they bet, you know the price before you commit. The player acting first has to decide blind to all of that. Over a single hand the difference is modest. Over thousands of hands it is enormous. Tracking databases from online poker show the same pattern for nearly every player: the button is their most profitable seat and the blinds are where they lose.
Control over the pot

Position also gives you control of the size of the pot. With a strong hand, you can bet when checked to and build it. With a medium hand, you can check behind and take a free card or a cheap showdown. With a draw, you decide whether to pay or to see the next card for nothing. Out of position you have none of these choices. If you check, your opponent decides. If you bet, you may be raised and forced into a guess.
Tight early, wide late

The practical result is that the hands worth playing change with your seat. In early position at a full table, with many players left to act behind you, a sound opening range is narrow, on the order of one hand in seven or eight. On the button, with only the blinds left to act, good players open something like four hands in ten. King nine suited is a clear fold under the gun and a routine raise on the button. The cards are identical. The seat changed their value.
Why the blinds lose

The blinds are a double handicap. You have put money in without seeing your cards, and you will be out of position for the rest of the hand. Even the best players in the world lose money from the blinds over time. The goal there is not to win but to lose less than the full blind you were forced to post. Defending too many weak hands from the blinds, on the theory that you already have chips invested, is a classic and costly habit.
Stealing

Because the button and cutoff act late, they often face a pot in which everyone has folded and only the blinds remain. Raising there with a wide range, called stealing the blinds, wins the pot outright a good share of the time. When it does not, the stealer still gets to play the hand in position. A player who folds the button too often is passing up the best seat at the table, and one who never defends the blinds is giving the stealer free money.
The simple rule

If you remember one thing about position, make it this: play more hands when you will act last and fewer when you will act first. When in doubt about a marginal hand, let your seat break the tie. Many players improve noticeably just by folding the weakest third of the hands they used to play from early position and adding that many on the button. No new skill is required. They are simply playing more of their pots with the advantage.
A check valve for electrons

A diode has two leads, the anode and the cathode. Current flows easily from anode to cathode and hardly at all the other way. On the part, a stripe marks the cathode end. On a schematic, the symbol is an arrow pointing at a bar, and the arrow shows the direction current is allowed to flow. Inside is a junction between two differently treated regions of silicon. The junction is the foundation of nearly all semiconductor devices, and a diode is the simplest thing you can build from one.
The forward drop

A diode is not a perfect valve. It needs a small voltage to open, and it keeps roughly that much for itself while conducting. For an ordinary silicon diode the figure is about 0.6 to 0.7 volts. Below it almost nothing flows. Above it the current rises steeply. That lost voltage becomes heat: a diode carrying 3 amps with 0.7 volts across it dissipates about 2 watts. Schottky diodes use a metal junction instead and drop only 0.2 to 0.4 volts, which is why they appear wherever efficiency matters.
Rectifying AC

The classic job is turning AC into DC. One diode passes only the positive half of the wave. Four diodes arranged in a diamond, called a bridge rectifier, steer both halves so they emerge pointing the same way. Follow that with a capacitor and you have rough DC. Every device that plugs into a wall contains this arrangement somewhere near its input. Bridge rectifiers are sold as single four-legged blocks marked with a wave symbol on two legs and plus and minus on the others.
Protecting against mistakes

A diode in series with a power input stops damage if the battery or adapter is connected backwards, at the cost of its forward drop. A diode across a relay coil absorbs the voltage spike when the coil is switched off. Two diodes from an input pin to the supply rails clamp any spike to a safe level, and most chips have these built in. Protection is unglamorous, but it is the reason modern gadgets survive static shocks and reversed plugs that would have destroyed electronics of fifty years ago.
Zener diodes work backwards on purpose

Every diode breaks down and conducts if enough reverse voltage is applied. A Zener diode is built so that this happens at a precise, repeatable voltage, such as 5.1 or 12 volts, without harming it. Wired in reverse with a resistor in series, it holds a steady voltage across itself while the input varies. It makes a simple voltage reference or a clamp that keeps a line from rising too high. For precision, a dedicated reference chip is better, but a Zener is cheap and nearly indestructible.
Light in, light out

Some diodes are built to interact with light. An LED emits light when current flows forward through it, with the colour set by the material. A photodiode does the reverse, producing a small current when light falls on it, and is the sensor in remote control receivers, smoke detectors and fibre optic links. A solar cell is a very large photodiode arranged to deliver power. All three are the same junction, optimized for a different job.
Testing a diode

Most multimeters have a diode setting, marked with the diode symbol. It pushes a small current through the part and shows the forward voltage. A good silicon diode reads about 0.5 to 0.7 one way and shows open circuit the other way. A reading near zero both ways means it has failed short. Open both ways means it has failed open. The same test checks the junctions inside a transistor, and with an LED it usually makes the part glow faintly, which conveniently tells you which lead is which.
Most hands miss

Start with a sobering fact. Two unpaired cards will make a pair or better on the flop only about one time in three. Two thirds of the time you have nothing but high cards. That is why starting hand selection matters so much. If you enter pots with weak cards, you will usually miss, and when you do hit, you will often hold a second best hand. Folding before the flop is the cheapest decision in the game, and good players do it most of the time.
Big pairs

Aces, kings and queens are the premium hands, strong enough to win unimproved. Their weakness is that they are usually still just one pair after the flop, and one pair loses big pots when the board turns ugly and the money goes in. The standard advice is to raise and reraise them before the flop, building a pot while you are a clear favourite and thinning the field. Slow playing aces against several opponents feels clever and often ends with a small win or a large loss.
Big cards and the kicker problem

Hands such as ace king and ace queen make top pair with a strong second card, called the kicker. That is their job. The danger lies in weaker versions. King jack and ace ten look good but are often dominated, meaning an opponent holds the same high card with a better kicker. When both players make top pair, the dominated hand pays off. Hands like these are where average players lose the most money, because the hand is too good to fold and not good enough to win.
Suited and connected

Being suited adds only a few percentage points to a hand's raw chance of winning. You will flop a flush just under one time in a hundred, and a flush draw about one time in nine. The value of suited connected cards such as 8 7 of hearts lies elsewhere. They make hidden straights and flushes that win big pots, and when they miss, they are easy to fold. They need deep stacks and good position to earn their keep.
Small pairs

Pairs from twos through sixes play one main way. You hope to flop three of a kind, which happens about one time in eight and a half. When it does, the hand is strong and well disguised. When it does not, you usually hold a low pair on a board of higher cards and should let it go. The discipline is the difficult part. A small pair that does not improve is rarely worth more than one cheap look.
Trouble hands

Certain hands have earned the name. Ace with a small unsuited card, king ten offsuit, queen jack offsuit against a raise from early position. They win small pots and lose large ones, because the hands that give them action are the hands that beat them. This does not make them unplayable. On the button, with everyone folded, they are fine raises. Against a raise from a tight player in early position, they are folds, however good they look.
A workable plan

Until you have studied ranges in detail, a simple scheme serves well. From early seats, play big pairs, ace king and ace queen. From the middle, add medium pairs and suited big cards. From the cutoff and button, add small pairs, suited connectors and suited aces. Enter the pot with a raise when you are first in. Fold the rest without regret. This plan is not optimal, but it avoids the common disasters, and it puts you ahead of most casual tables.
A diode that glows

A light emitting diode is a diode made from materials that release light when current crosses the junction. The colour depends on the material, not on any coating. Red and green LEDs appeared in the 1960s and 70s. An efficient blue one arrived only in the early 1990s, work that earned Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics. Blue made white light possible, by coating a blue LED with a phosphor that converts part of its output to yellow.
Voltage is set by colour

Each colour has its own forward voltage. Red runs at about 1.8 to 2.2 volts. Yellow and older green are similar. Blue, white and modern bright green need about 3 to 3.3 volts. This is a property of the part, and you cannot change it. It means a 3 volt coin cell lights a red LED easily and a blue one only barely, and that a red and a blue LED wired directly in parallel will not share: the red one takes nearly all the current.
Why it needs a resistor

Once an LED reaches its forward voltage, a tiny further increase in voltage produces a huge increase in current. Connect one straight to a supply and nothing limits that current except the supply itself. The LED overheats and fails in a fraction of a second, sometimes with a pop. A series resistor absorbs the difference between the supply and the forward voltage and so fixes the current. Subtract the LED's voltage from the supply, divide by the current you want, and you have the value.
How much current to give it

A standard indicator LED is rated for 20 milliamps, but modern ones are so efficient that 1 to 5 milliamps is plenty for a status light indoors. Running at a fraction of the rating saves power and extends life. High power LEDs for lighting are a different animal, running at 350 milliamps to several amps. Those need a constant current driver circuit and a heatsink. A resistor would waste too much power and would not hold the current steady as the LED warms up.
Which leg is which

An LED only lights one way round. On a new through-hole part the longer leg is the anode, the positive side. The plastic rim usually has a flat spot beside the cathode, the negative side. Inside the lens, the larger metal piece is generally the cathode. Surface mount LEDs carry a green mark or a notch at the cathode end. Connecting an ordinary LED backwards at low voltage does not hurt it. It simply stays dark, which makes reversed polarity the first thing to check.
Dimming without changing colour

Lowering the current dims an LED, but the colour of white LEDs shifts slightly as it drops. The preferred method is to switch the LED fully on and fully off very fast and vary the fraction of time it is on. Above a few hundred times a second the eye sees a steady, dimmer light. The technique is called pulse width modulation. Poorly designed dimmers switch too slowly, which is the flicker some people notice in cheap bulbs and car tail lights when their eyes move.
What actually kills them

LEDs do not burn out like filaments. They fade, and heat is the cause. An LED's rated life, often 25,000 hours or more, is the time until its output falls to 70 percent, assuming it is kept cool. In a household bulb the LEDs themselves usually outlast the cramped, hot driver electronics packed in the base. That is why a bulb in an enclosed fixture fails early, and why the first sign of death is often flickering instead of darkness.
What a limp is

To limp is to enter the pot before the flop by calling the big blind, not raising. Players do it because it costs little and lets them see a flop with a hand they like but do not love. It is the most common play at casual tables and nearly absent from strong ones. When the first player into the pot has a hand worth playing, the better play is almost always a raise. When the hand is not worth a raise, it is usually not worth playing.
A raise can win now

The first argument is simple. A limp cannot win the pot before the flop. A raise can. Every time everyone folds, the raiser collects the blinds without seeing a card. Those small pots add up to a real share of a winning player's profit. A limper gives up that entire source of income and must always make the best hand, or bluff later at greater expense, to win anything at all.
Initiative

The player who made the last aggressive action before the flop holds what is called the initiative. Opponents tend to check to that player on the flop, and a bet from them is believable, because raising before the flop represents a strong hand. This lets the raiser win many pots with a single follow-up bet when nobody has connected. A limper has shown no strength, so a later bet tells a weaker story, and opponents call it more freely.
Fewer opponents, clearer hands

A raise thins the field. Against one opponent, a pair of kings wins about four times in five against a random hand. Against four opponents holding random hands, it wins only about half the time. Limping invites a crowd, and in a crowd even good hands shrink, because somebody usually makes two pair or better. A raise also narrows what the callers can hold, since most players continue against a raise with only their better hands. That makes the rest of the hand easier to read.
Limps invite attacks

At a table with observant players, a limp is a target. It announces a hand that is good enough to play but not good enough to raise. Players behind can raise with a wide range, knowing the limper will usually fold or call and then play out of position with a marginal hand. Over time, limpers pay the blind repeatedly and surrender it repeatedly. A limp is too weak to defend and too expensive to keep abandoning. Watch any table for an hour and note who limps most often. It is rarely the player with the biggest stack at the end of the night.
How much to raise

A standard opening raise is between two and a half and three times the big blind. In live games where players call more loosely, slightly larger is common. If players have already limped in front of you, add about one big blind for each of them. Keep your raise size the same whether you hold aces or a speculative hand. Varying your bet with the strength of your cards gives attentive opponents a free read on your hand.
The exceptions

There are narrow cases where limping is defensible. In the small blind, with only the big blind left to act, a mixed approach of calls and raises is sound. In very passive games where nobody ever raises, limping behind other limpers with a small pair or suited connector can be profitable, because you are getting a good price in a multi-player pot. These are exceptions for specific situations. As a default, the rule holds: if you are the first to enter the pot, raise or fold.
Three legs, one job

A bipolar junction transistor has three terminals: base, collector and emitter. A small current flowing into the base allows a much larger current to flow from collector to emitter. With no base current, the path is closed. The ratio between the two currents is the gain, typically 100 or more for a small transistor. So a microcontroller pin that can supply only a few milliamps can, through a transistor, control a motor, a relay or a strip of lights drawing a hundred times as much.
NPN and PNP

Transistors come in two polarities. An NPN transistor turns on when its base is driven positive relative to its emitter and is used to switch the ground side of a load. A PNP transistor is the mirror image, turning on when its base is pulled below its emitter, and switches the positive side. Beginners should start with NPN, since it matches the way logic outputs work: pin high, load on. The common 2N3904 and its cousin the 2N2222 are NPN parts that have been in production for more than half a century.
The standard switch circuit

Connect the load between the positive supply and the collector. Connect the emitter to ground. Connect the control pin to the base through a resistor. When the pin goes high, current flows through the resistor into the base, the transistor conducts and the load turns on. The resistor is essential. The base behaves like a diode to ground, and without a resistor the pin would try to supply unlimited current into it. A value of 1 kilohm suits most small loads driven from 5 volts.
Saturation: fully on

For switching, you want the transistor fully on, a state called saturation, where the voltage left across it is only about 0.2 volts. To guarantee that, supply noticeably more base current than the gain calculation strictly requires. A common rule is to assume a gain of only 10 or 20. For a 100 milliamp load, that means 5 to 10 milliamps into the base. A transistor that is only partly on drops several volts while carrying current, so it runs hot and may fail.
Protecting it from the load

Loads with coils, such as relays, motors and solenoids, kick back with a high voltage spike when switched off. Place a diode across the load with its stripe toward the positive supply and the spike circulates harmlessly. Leave it out and the transistor may work for days before failing, which makes the fault hard to connect to its cause. This diode is the most often forgotten part in beginner circuits, and adding it costs a couple of cents.
When to use something else

A small bipolar transistor is right for loads up to a few hundred milliamps. Beyond that, the base current needed becomes awkward and the 0.2 volt drop starts to waste real power. The usual step up is a MOSFET, which is controlled by voltage and wastes far less at high current. For switching mains voltage or providing complete electrical isolation, use a relay or a solid state relay, with the transistor driving the relay's coil.
Billions of the same idea

The switch you can hold between two fingers is the same idea, in different form, as the ones in a processor. The first transistor was demonstrated at Bell Labs in December 1947 and was about the size of a thumb. A modern phone chip contains well over ten billion, each a switch turning the next one on or off. Logic gates, memory cells and arithmetic units are all arrangements of switches. Understand one transistor switching one LED and you hold the bottom rung of the ladder that leads to every computer.
Why it is called a 3-bet

The big blind counts as the first bet. An opening raise is the second. A reraise over that is therefore the third bet, or 3-bet. A further raise is a 4-bet. Decades ago, players reraised before the flop only with aces and kings, and everyone knew it. Modern players 3-bet a much wider set of hands, some for value and some as bluffs. Learning to do it, and to respond to it, is one of the clearest dividing lines between beginners and experienced players.
For value

The obvious reason to 3-bet is that you hold a hand that beats most of what the raiser has. With aces, kings, queens and ace king, you want more money in the pot while you are ahead. Just calling with these hands keeps the pot small and lets other players enter cheaply behind you, which reduces your chance of winning. Against opponents who raise many hands and dislike folding, the value range can widen to jacks, tens and ace queen.
As a bluff

If you only reraise with premium hands, good opponents simply fold everything but their own premiums. So strong players add bluffs. The best candidates are hands that are not quite good enough to call but have useful features. Small suited aces such as ace five of spades are the classic choice. The ace in your hand makes it less likely your opponent holds aces or ace king, and if you are called, the hand can still make the best flush or a hidden straight.
Sizing

A 3-bet should be large enough that calling is unattractive. A common guide is about three times the original raise when you will have position after the flop, and about four times when you will be out of position, because acting first is a handicap you want to offset by ending the hand sooner. If the opener raised to 3 big blinds, that means roughly 9 from the button and 12 from the blinds. Tiny reraises simply give the opener a great price to call.
Who to target

The 3-bet works best against players who open too many hands and fold too many of them to pressure. Someone raising from late position with a wide range cannot defend most of it against a reraise. It works poorly against players who only raise strong hands, since their range is already full of hands that will not fold, and poorly against players who call everything, where you should reraise only for value and skip the bluffs entirely.
Facing a 3-bet

When you are the one reraised, three questions sort it out. How often does this player 3-bet? Against a rare 3-bettor, fold everything but the very top of your range. Will you have position? Calling out of position with a marginal hand is expensive. And how deep are the stacks? With deep stacks, calling with pairs and suited connectors is reasonable. With shallow stacks, the choice narrows to fold or move all in, because there is no room to manoeuvre afterwards.
What changes after the flop

A 3-bet pot is larger relative to the stacks behind, so decisions come faster and for more money. A single bet on the flop and one on the turn can put a player all in. Top pair is often strong enough to commit with, which it would not be in a small pot. The player who 3-bet also has the stronger range, so bets from that player carry more weight on boards with high cards. All of this follows from one reraise before the flop.
